clue.text: A bit soft, maybe, but so mature!

definitions.text: A bit soft, maybe, but so mature!

parts.words: A bit soft, maybe, but so mature
parts.note: fruit that has gone a little squashy is past its best because it has ripened too far

explanation.surface: A grudging remark about something gentle yet grown-up.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruit that has gone too far past ripeness turns soft, so softness here is a sign of excessive maturity.

clue.text: Lone deep groan is emitted by citizen

indicators.note: a groan let out comes out jumbled, so these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A lonely person lets out a deep groan beside a fellow citizen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is emitted' tells you to rearrange LONE DEEP GROAN. The definition is thin; the printed clue probably read 'senior citizen'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pensioner of retirement age is a senior member of the community, the sense the clue gives as citizen.

clue.text: Even very, intemperate clattering contains a striking effect

indicators.note: the phrase holds a run of letters inside it, straddling the two words

explanation.surface: A loud, uncontrolled racket does at least make an impression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contains' points to letters running across the end of 'intemperate' and the start of 'clattering'.
explanation.definitionFit: Éclat is brilliant display or dazzling success, a striking effect borrowed from French.

clue.text: Resolved after check to carry on same policy.

indicators.note: after places the resolved word behind the check word

parts.note: to check a horse is to rein it in
resolved means sure, certain in one's mind

explanation.surface: Having thought it over, someone decides to keep their insurance cover unchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: To insure again with the same cover is to continue an existing policy with an insurer.

clue.text: Blab in a soft manner.

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning soft
rate can mean manner or fashion, as in 'at any rate'

explanation.surface: Someone tells secrets but does so gently.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean to chatter on foolishly, giving away more than one should.

clue.text: Circulates free tickets.

definitions.meaning: moves around from hand to hand

explanation.surface: Someone hands out complimentary tickets.
explanation.definitionFit: Something circulating is handed round from person to person; complimentary tickets let holders in without paying.

clue.text: To that extent, a carrier is in a lost

parts.note: as means to that degree, as in 'as tall'
a tray is something used for carrying things

explanation.surface: A carrier seems to have lost its way.
explanation.definitionFit: Going off the right path means being lost or having wandered away.

clue.text: The consciousness one put into ment.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'The consciousness one put into ment.': the last word is cut short (probably a word for SENTENCE such as 'punishment'), more than an OCR slip, and no scan is available.
annotationWithheld.clue: The consciousness one put into ment.

clue.text: Puppets usually have such awkward conditions associated with them.

definitions.text: Puppets usually have such awkward conditions associated with them.

parts.words: Puppets usually have such awkward conditions associated with them
parts.note: marionettes hang from cords, and a deal with hidden obligations is said to have cords fastened to it

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means conditions or catches that come with an offer, pictured as the cords controlling a marionette.

clue.text: Maori can make this dish.

indicators.note: make suggests the letters are worked into something new

explanation.surface: A New Zealander says they are able to cook a certain dish.
explanation.definitionFit: Macaroni is a tube-shaped pasta served as a dish.

clue.text: A boy returns with a mail package Eastern leader.

indicators.note: a boy coming back is read in reverse, from right to left

parts.note: a lad is a boy

indicators.note: the letters are packaged up in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A boy comes home bringing a parcel of post for a leader from the East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returns' turns A LAD into DALA; 'package' rearranges A MAIL into ILAMA.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dalai Lama is the spiritual head of Tibetan Buddhism, a leader in Asia.

clue.text: General course for singer.

definitions.meaning: the overall drift or gist of something
a male voice between baritone and alto

explanation.surface: An army general's route is taken by a vocalist.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenor means the gist or prevailing direction of something, and also a high male voice.

clue.text: "Battering the of heaven storms of prayer." (Tennyson)

definitions.text: "Battering the of heaven storms of prayer." (Tennyson)

parts.words: Battering the of heaven storms of prayer
parts.note: a quotation from Tennyson with one word left out; the missing word is the entrances of heaven

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: the full line reads 'Battering the gates of heaven with storms of prayer'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennyson's line speaks of prayers hammering at the entrances of heaven, the word missing from the quotation.

clue.text: Half the cinema people simply gas!

indicators.note: only the back half of the following word is kept

parts.note: a nation is a people

explanation.surface: Someone complains that half the cinema audience is just hot air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half the' keeps the last three letters of CINEMA, EMA.
explanation.definitionFit: An emanation is something given off, such as a vapour or fumes.

clue.text: Man who spins out the time gives you all the angles?

definitions.text: Man who spins out the time
definitions.meaning: one who prolongs or drags out proceedings
an instrument for measuring angles in geometry

explanation.surface: A time-waster seems to know every trick.
explanation.definitionFit: To protract is to prolong, so one who does so drags things out; the geometry instrument measures angles.

clue.text: As decreed, I've taken my place amid the artillery.

indicators.note: the speaker has settled inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: ordnance means artillery, heavy guns
I, the speaker, gives the letter I

explanation.surface: Under orders, a soldier has taken position among the big guns.
explanation.definitionFit: An ordinance is an authoritative decree or order, so the clue's phrase points to something laid down by authority.

clue.text: In vulgar fashion usually.

explanation.surface: Someone usually behaves crudely.
explanation.definitionFit: Common can mean coarse or low-class, and also ordinary or frequent, so the adverb covers both.

clue.text: Take responsibility for upsetting of light and love.

indicators.note: upsetting turns the combined pieces round, so they read backwards

parts.note: the sun gives light
love is zero in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone takes the blame for knocking over a lamp and a lover.
explanation.definitionFit: An onus is a burden or duty that someone must bear.

clue.text: Prickly plant placed in a tin accordingly.

parts.note: a can is a tin
thus means accordingly, therefore

explanation.surface: A spiky plant has been potted in a tin as instructed.
explanation.definitionFit: Acanthus is a spiny-leaved plant, its leaves the model for Corinthian column decoration.

clue.text: Agrees, apparently, but commits

clue.text: "The sculptur'd dead on each side seem to" (Keats)

definitions.text: "The sculptur'd dead on each side seem to" (Keats)

parts.words: The sculptur'd dead on each side seem to
parts.note: a line from Keats's Eve of St Agnes with its last word missing, the stone effigies seeming to turn icy

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation from The Eve of St Agnes, set on a bitterly cold night.
explanation.definitionFit: In Keats's poem the carved stone figures in the chapel seem to turn rigid with cold, the missing final word.

clue.text: Deep-down exactly.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Deep-down exactly.': 'exactly' has no job in any parse, so the clue appears garbled or cut short, and no scan is available.

clue.text: Way out west, a strap used for punishment!

indicators.note: way out suggests letters gone astray and rearranged

explanation.surface: Far off in the west, a strap is kept for discipline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Way out' rearranges WEST A. Pun on 'way out west', the Scottish setting where this leather strap was used in schools.
explanation.definitionFit: A tawse is a leather belt with split ends once used to beat pupils in Scottish schools.

clue.text: Just the reverse of a home girl?

indicators.note: the order of the two words is swapped, so the home comes before the a

parts.note: a nest is a bird's home

explanation.surface: A homebody girl is described as the opposite of house-proud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a home' is A NEST; 'Just the reverse' swaps the words to NEST A, a girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Nesta is a Welsh female first name.

clue.text: More confident of finding northern river among the tracks of the south?

indicators.note: among puts the river between the railway letters

parts.note: SR was the Southern Railway, the railway lines of southern England
the Ure is a river in North Yorkshire

explanation.surface: Someone is more certain of finding a northern river beside southern railway lines.
explanation.definitionFit: Surer is the comparative of sure, meaning more certain.

clue.text: Having a particular purpose in Shakespeare for the time being.

definitions.text: Having a particular purpose in Shakespeare
definitions.meaning: in Shakespeare 'for the ...' means for a particular purpose

explanation.surface: In Shakespeare's plays something is done with intent, but only temporarily.
explanation.definitionFit: The word survives in 'for the nonce', meaning for now, and in Elizabethan use meant for a specific purpose.

clue.text: Evangelical house of worship spire?

definitions.meaning: the ... wing of Anglicanism is evangelical
read literally, a church with a short spire

explanation.surface: An evangelical church has a modest spire.
explanation.definitionFit: Low church means the evangelical wing of the Church of England, and literally pictures a church building that is short in height.

clue.text: Staggered, yet brought the fish in?

definitions.meaning: wound in the line on an angler's spool

explanation.surface: An angler tottered but still landed the catch.
explanation.definitionFit: To reel is to stagger dizzily, and also to wind in a fishing line on its spool.

clue.text: Describing a slow and heavy step tain in the field.
